```{r setup, include = FALSE}
library(multiScaleR)
library(terra)

knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment  = "#>",
  fig.width  = 6.5,
  fig.height = 4.25,
  warning  = FALSE,
  message  = FALSE
)

# Three fits are stored in the package so the vignette builds quickly. The text
# shows the real calls.
# - N-mixture model (about four minutes): inst/extdata/opt_umf_p.rds, made by
#   data-raw/generate_pcount_vignette_object.R
# - Zero-inflated and occupancy models (about 20 s together):
#   inst/extdata/multiScaleR_Guide-cache.rds, made by
#   data-raw/cache_multiScaleR_Guide.R
# Every other model in this vignette runs when it is built.
stored_file <- function(name) {
  path <- file.path("..", "inst", "extdata", name)
  if (!file.exists(path)) {
    path <- system.file("extdata", name, package = "multiScaleR")
  }
  path
}
opt_nmix_stored <- readRDS(stored_file("opt_umf_p.rds"))
guide_cache     <- readRDS(stored_file("multiScaleR_Guide-cache.rds"))
```

# What this vignette covers

How far from a survey point does the landscape still matter, and how sure can
you be of that distance? `vignette("quickstart", package = "multiScaleR")`
answers the question for one count model. This guide is the full tour of the
same workflow. It explains what the kernel parameters mean, which settings of
`kernel_prep()` and `multiScale_optim()` matter, how to tell a well-estimated
scale from a poorly estimated one, and how to compare candidate models.

You will fit the Quick Start model again with one covariate too many, find
that covariate from the output, and remove it. You will then fit negative
binomial, zero-inflated, binary occurrence, N-mixture, and occupancy models,
and map a fitted model. Read the Quick Start first. This guide assumes you can
fit a generalized linear model with `glm()` and read a raster with `terra`.

# Know what the package estimates

The *scale of effect* is the distance over which a landscape variable
influences a response measured at a survey location. Suppose you model
songbird abundance and expect forest cover around each point to matter. Should
you measure forest within 100 m, 500 m, or 2 km? The usual answer is to fit
one model per candidate buffer radius and keep the best. That approach has two
limits. The true scale can fall between the radii you tried, and a buffer
gives a forest patch 499 m away the same weight as one 50 m away.

`multiScaleR` replaces the buffer with a *kernel*, a function that gives
nearby raster cells more weight than distant ones. The kernel width, sigma, is
in map units and sets how quickly the weight declines with distance. Sigma is
estimated from your data together with the regression coefficients, so each
scale of effect comes with a standard error and a confidence interval.

Bayesian frameworks can also estimate scales of effect (e.g., Stuber & Gruber
2020; Amirkhiz et al. 2023), and the R packages `Siland` (Carpentier & Martin
2021) and `Scalescape` (Lowe et al. 2022) estimate distance-weighted landscape
effects. `multiScaleR` supports models of class `glm`, `glm.nb`, `nlme`
(including `gls`), `lme4`, and many `unmarkedFit` classes. Other model classes
may work when they have a suitable `update()` method and are supported by the
[insight](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=insight) package.

# Understand the kernel and its parameters

## Choose a kernel

Four kernels are available. In each, sigma sets the width. The exponential
power kernel has a second parameter that sets the shape of the curve.

| Kernel | `kernel =` | Weight of a cell at distance *d* | Parameters estimated |
|:-------|:-----------|:---------------------------------|:---------------------|
| Gaussian | `"gaussian"` | exp(-*d*^2^ / (2 sigma^2^)) | sigma |
| Negative exponential | `"exp"` | exp(-*d* / sigma) | sigma |
| Exponential power | `"expow"` | exp(-(*d* / sigma)^shape^) | sigma and shape |
| Fixed buffer | `"fixed"` | Equal within the radius, zero beyond it | radius |

```{r kernel-shapes, fig.height = 5.5, fig.cap = "***Weight against distance for the four kernels, each drawn with sigma = 300 m. The dashed line marks the radius that holds 90% of the kernel weight.***"}
library(ggplot2)   # adds a title to each panel
library(cowplot)   # arranges the four panels on one page

# plot_kernel() draws a kernel without a fitted model.
# add_label = FALSE leaves out the text under each panel.
k_gaus  <- plot_kernel(sigma = 300, kernel = "gaussian", add_label = FALSE)
k_exp   <- plot_kernel(sigma = 300, kernel = "exp",      add_label = FALSE)
k_expow <- plot_kernel(sigma = 300, kernel = "expow",    add_label = FALSE,
                       shape = 5)         # shape of the exponential power curve
k_fixed <- plot_kernel(sigma = 300, kernel = "fixed",    add_label = FALSE)

plot_grid(k_gaus  + ggtitle("Gaussian"),
          k_exp   + ggtitle("Negative exponential"),
          k_expow + ggtitle("Exponential power, shape 5"),
          k_fixed + ggtitle("Fixed buffer"))
```

**How to read these plots:** Each curve shows the weight a raster cell
receives at a given distance from the survey point. The Gaussian curve stays
high near the point and then falls smoothly. The negative exponential drops
fastest close to the point and keeps a long tail, so the horizontal axis of
that panel runs much farther. A large shape value turns the exponential power
kernel into a plateau with a steep edge, which approaches the fixed buffer.

Start with the Gaussian kernel, which is the default. The exponential power
kernel is the most flexible, but in simulations it is prone to overfitting and
its optimization can fail to converge. Reserve the other kernels for cases
where you have a biological reason to test a different decay shape, and
compare them with the Gaussian fit as shown in [Compare kernels].

## Convert sigma to an effective distance

Sigma is a parameter, not a radius. The same sigma means a different reach
under each kernel, so report the *effective distance*, the radius of the
circle around a point that holds a stated share of the kernel weight (90% by
default). `kernel_dist()` does the conversion, with or without a fitted model.

```{r kernel-dist}
# Radius (m) of the circle holding 90% of the weight, sigma = 300 m
kernel_dist(sigma = 300, kernel = "gaussian")
kernel_dist(sigma = 300, kernel = "exp")

# The same Gaussian kernel with 95% of the weight
kernel_dist(sigma = 300, kernel = "gaussian", prob = 0.95)

# Line-based definition: distance holding 90% of the weight along a transect
kernel_dist(sigma = 300, kernel = "gaussian", dimension = "1d")
```

**How to read the output:** A Gaussian kernel with sigma = 300 m places 90% of
its weight within about 644 m, or 2.15 times sigma. A negative exponential
kernel with the same sigma reaches about 1,167 m. The last line uses an older
definition that measures along a line through the point and gives a shorter
distance, about 1.65 times sigma. The circle is the default because rings
farther from a point contain more cells. Whichever you report, state the
definition and the share of weight.

An effective distance describes an ideal kernel on an unbounded plane. The
share of weight your data actually used can differ near a raster edge, around
missing cells, or when `max_D` cuts the kernel short.

# Prepare the data

## Load the running example

This guide uses the data from the Quick Start. Counts at 100 survey points
were simulated from two of three landscape layers.

```{r load-data}
data("landscape_counts")   # counts and one site-level covariate, 100 rows
dat <- landscape_counts

data("surv_pts")           # survey locations (an sf object from the package)
pts <- vect(surv_pts)      # convert to a terra SpatVector

# Three landscape layers on one 20 m grid
land_rast <- rast(system.file("extdata", "landscape.tif",
                              package = "multiScaleR"))
```

| Quantity | True value |
|:---------|:-----------|
| Intercept, on the log scale | 0.25 |
| Effect of `site`, a covariate measured at the survey point | 0.3 |
| Effect and sigma of `land1`, a binary habitat layer | -0.5, 250 m |
| Effect and sigma of `land2`, a continuous layer | 0.7, 500 m |
| `land3`, a continuous layer | No effect |

## Extract the landscape around each point

`kernel_prep()` does two jobs. It extracts every raster cell within `max_D`
map units of each survey point, along with the distance to that cell. It then
computes a first set of kernel-weighted covariates from a starting sigma of
`max_D / 2`, which you use to fit the starting model.

```{r kernel-prep}
kernel_inputs <- kernel_prep(
  pts          = pts,          # survey locations
  raster_stack = land_rast,    # landscape layers to summarize
  max_D        = 1700,         # largest distance (m) searched around a point
  kernel       = "gaussian",   # shape of the distance-decay function
  verbose      = FALSE
)
kernel_inputs
```

**How to read the output:** The object holds 100 survey points and three
covariates, one per raster layer. "Number of elements" counts the raster cells
extracted around the first survey point. The minimum distance is the cell size
(20 m) and the maximum distance is your `max_D`. The optimizer searches for
sigma between those two distances.

The arguments below carry the decisions that matter.

| Argument | Default | What it controls |
|:---------|:--------|:-----------------|
| `max_D` | None | The search limit, in map units. Set it beyond any scale you consider plausible. If `multiScale_optim()` warns that an estimate is near `max_D`, increase it and run `kernel_prep()` again |
| `kernel` | `"gaussian"` | The decay function. It is fixed here, so comparing kernels means one `kernel_prep()` call per kernel |
| `bin` | `TRUE` | Summarizes the extracted cells into distance bins. The optimizer then works with the bins, so its speed no longer depends on `max_D`. `bin = FALSE` forces the exact cell-by-cell calculation |
| `nbins` | `256` | Number of distance bins. The default reproduces the exact estimates to several significant figures |
| `store_cell_data` | `TRUE` | Keeps the cell values after binning. `FALSE` keeps only the bins, which is enough to optimize, profile, and project |
| `sigma` | `max_D / 2` | Starting sigma for each covariate, in map units. The default is recommended |

A large `max_D` costs extraction time and memory, not optimization time. If
memory is the constraint, drop the cell values.

```{r lean-prep}
# Same preparation, keeping only the distance bins
lean_inputs <- kernel_prep(pts = pts, raster_stack = land_rast,
                           max_D = 1700, kernel = "gaussian",
                           store_cell_data = FALSE, verbose = FALSE)

# Size of each object in megabytes
c(full = as.numeric(object.size(kernel_inputs)),
  lean = as.numeric(object.size(lean_inputs))) / 1e6
```

**How to read the output:** The lean object is a small fraction of the full
one. Lean storage is available only when every covariate is kernel-weighted.
Landscape and surface metrics need the cell values, and `kernel_prep()` keeps
them automatically (see
`vignette("landscape_metric_covariates", package = "multiScaleR")`). For
surveys from several years with a different map each year, use
`kernel_prep_by_group()` as shown in
`vignette("year-specific-rasters", package = "multiScaleR")`.

# Fit the model

## Fit a starting model

The kernel-weighted covariates are in `kernel_inputs$kernel_dat`, centered and
scaled to a mean of zero and a standard deviation of one. Combine them with
the response and fit the model you intend to optimize. `multiScale_optim()`
inherits its formula, family, and any random effects, so settle the model
structure here. The Quick Start fitted the two layers that affect the counts.
This model adds `land3`, which does not.

```{r start-model}
df <- data.frame(dat, kernel_inputs$kernel_dat)

# Starting model with all three landscape layers
mod_full <- glm(counts ~ site + land1 + land2 + land3,
                family = poisson(),
                data   = df)
```

Write the formula directly in the fitting call. The package refits the model
many times, and a formula or data set that exists only inside a function or
loop may not be found again. When you need full control of the refit, pass
your own function through the `refit_fn` argument of `multiScale_optim()`.

## Estimate the scales of effect

```{r optim-full}
opt_full <- multiScale_optim(fitted_mod    = mod_full,
                             kernel_inputs = kernel_inputs,
                             verbose       = FALSE)   # no progress messages
```

The search starts every sigma at `max_D / 2` unless you supply starting values
or request screened starts (see [Choose a start strategy]). This fit takes
under a second. Slower models, such as mixed or `unmarked` models, can run in
parallel with `n_cores`. Each worker holds its own copy of the inputs, so
check the memory cost first.

```{r ram, eval = FALSE}
# Estimated memory for three workers, and the largest safe worker count
estimate_multiscale_ram(kernel_inputs, fitted_mod = mod_full, n_cores = 3)
```

The report gives a recommended maximum number of workers and a peak memory
estimate for the count you requested. `multiScale_optim()` stops with an error
when `n_cores` exceeds the limit set by available memory. It does not lower
the count for you. Preparing the inputs with `store_cell_data = FALSE` is the
usual way to bring a large problem under the limit.

# Read the summary

```{r summary-full}
summary(opt_full)
```

**How to read the `summary()` output:** The Quick Start describes the four
blocks. Here, attention goes to the parts that flag a problem.

- **Standard errors and intervals for sigma.** For `land1` and `land2` the
  standard error is a small fraction of the estimate. For `land3` it is more
  than half the estimate, and the interval runs from the cell size to more
  than 1,100 m. The data say almost nothing about the scale of `land3`.
- **Two distance tables.** The table marked "selected" is the radius of the
  circle that holds 90% of the kernel weight. The second is the line-based
  definition from [Convert sigma to an effective distance]. Both come from the
  same sigma. `summary(opt_full)$opt_dist_2d` and `$opt_dist_1d` return them
  by name if a script needs one definition regardless of the display.
- **Warnings.** The first warning reports that an effective distance
  approaches the search limit and gives the `max_D` that would cover it. The
  second names the precision problem, a sigma standard error that is at least
  50% of its estimate.
- **Follow-up recommendation.** These are the `max_D` and starting sigma
  values to use if you refit.

A sigma that drifts toward `max_D` with a wide interval has two possible
causes. Either the true scale is larger than the area you extracted, or the
covariate has little or no relationship with the response. To tell them apart,
look at the regression table. The coefficient for `land3` is small, and its
standard error is more than half its size. A covariate without an effect gives
the optimizer nothing to hold onto, and sigma wanders.

## Remove a covariate the data do not support

Because the data are simulated, you know that `land3` has no effect. With real
data you would reach the same decision from the summary above, the profile in
[Check how well each scale is identified], and the model comparison in
[Compare models].

```{r optim-reduced}
# Starting model without land3 (the Quick Start model)
mod <- glm(counts ~ site + land1 + land2,
           family = poisson(),
           data   = df)

opt <- multiScale_optim(fitted_mod    = mod,
                        kernel_inputs = kernel_inputs,
                        verbose       = FALSE)

opt$scale_est                      # sigma and its standard error, in meters
round(kernel_dist(opt))            # radius holding 90% of the kernel weight (m)
round(exp(coef(opt$opt_mod)), 2)   # multiplicative change in expected count
```

**How to read the output:** No warnings remain. The sigma estimates of
`r round(opt$scale_est["land1", "Mean"])` m and
`r round(opt$scale_est["land2", "Mean"])` m sit close to the true values of
250 m and 500 m. In distance terms, `land1` acts within about
`r round(kernel_dist(opt)["land1", "Mean"])` m of a survey point and `land2`
within about `r format(round(kernel_dist(opt)["land2", "Mean"]), big.mark = ",")` m.
The landscape covariates are standardized, so each coefficient describes a
change of one standard deviation. One standard deviation more kernel-weighted
`land1` multiplies the expected count by
`r round(exp(coef(opt$opt_mod))["land1"], 2)`, and the same increase in `land2`
multiplies it by `r round(exp(coef(opt$opt_mod))["land2"], 2)`.

## Choose an interval for sigma

By default, the sigma interval comes from the *delta method*. It uses the
curvature of the likelihood at the estimate and assumes the likelihood is
symmetric around it. A *profile-likelihood interval* makes no such assumption.
It moves sigma away from the estimate, refits the other parameters at each
step, and stops where the log-likelihood has dropped by 1.92 units, the cutoff
for a 95% interval.

```{r profile-interval}
# Delta-method limits (the default), in meters
round(summary(opt)$opt_scale)

# Profile-likelihood limits. The standard error column does not change
round(summary(opt, profile = TRUE)$opt_scale)
```

**How to read the output:** The two methods nearly agree on the lower limit
for `land1`. The profile-likelihood upper limit is about 15 m higher, because
the likelihood falls away more slowly above the estimate than below it. For
`land2` both limits move up by about 10 m. A symmetric interval cannot show
either pattern.

Request profile-likelihood intervals when

- an estimate is near `max_D`,
- the delta-method interval is wide relative to the estimate,
- the sample is small (fewer than about 75 sites), or
- you will report the interval in a manuscript.

For a fixed-buffer kernel, a landscape metric, or an unweighted surface
metric, the likelihood changes in steps as whole cells enter the neighborhood.
Curvature is not a useful measure there, and the summary shows `NA` for the
standard error and interval. Inspect the profile from `profile_sigma()`
instead. `vignette("inference-contracts", package = "multiScaleR")` explains
what each interval includes and what it leaves out.

> **What this means for your study.** A wide sigma interval is a result, not a
> nuisance. It tells you that the data cannot separate a local effect from a
> broad one for that covariate. Report the interval, and do not build an
> ecological explanation on the point estimate alone.

# Plot the kernels and the effects

```{r plot-kernels, fig.cap = "***Fitted kernels for `land1` and `land2`.***"}
plot(opt)
```

**How to read these plots:** Each panel is the fitted version of the curves in
[Choose a kernel]. The dashed line is the effective distance and the gray band
is its 95% confidence interval. Three lines of text sit under each panel. The
first states the share of kernel weight and the distance definition. The
second gives sigma and the effective distance, and the third gives the 95%
confidence interval for that distance. Keep in mind that the dashed line marks
a radius. It does not split the area under the plotted curve 90 to 10.

The text helps while you explore a fit. For a manuscript figure, set
`add_label = FALSE` to remove it. The line and the band stay.

```{r plot-kernels-99, fig.cap = "***The same kernels with the radius that holds 99% of the weight, and no text under the panels.***"}
# prob changes the share of weight. dimension = "1d" gives the line-based distance
plot(opt, prob = 0.99, add_label = FALSE)
```

`plot_marginal_effects()` draws the expected response across each covariate,
with the other covariates held at their means.

```{r marginal, fig.cap = "***Expected count across each covariate in the reduced model.***"}
plot_marginal_effects(opt)
```

**How to read these plots:** The vertical axis is the expected count. The
horizontal axis is the covariate in its own units, which for `land1` is the
kernel-weighted proportion of habitat around a point. Counts fall as habitat
within the fitted kernel increases and rise with `land2`. The shaded band is a
95% confidence band that treats the estimated scales as known.

# Check how well each scale is identified

`profile_sigma()` refits the model across a grid of sigma values for one
covariate at a time, holding the other scales at their estimates. The grid is
log-spaced by default, with more values at small scales where the fit changes
fastest. Profiling the full model shows what an unidentified scale looks like.

```{r profile, fig.cap = "***AICc across candidate sigma values for each covariate in the full model. The dashed line marks the estimate.***"}
prof_full <- profile_sigma(opt_full, n_pts = 15,   # 15 sigma values per covariate
                           verbose = FALSE)
plot(prof_full)
```

**How to read these plots:** Lower AICc means better support. Read the
vertical axis before the shape of the curve. For `land1` and `land2`, AICc
rises by tens of units on either side of a clear minimum, so the data identify
those scales. For `land3` the curve also has a minimum, but the whole axis
spans less than two AICc units. Every sigma between the cell size and `max_D`
fits about equally well.

Use this rule. A trough several AICc units deep near the dashed line means the
scale is identified. A flat profile means the data do not constrain that
scale. When the profile keeps falling toward `max_D`, the search limit set the
estimate and the data did not. With several covariates, `n_cores` profiles them
in parallel.

# Choose a start strategy

The optimizer follows the likelihood uphill from its starting values. When the
likelihood has several peaks or flat steps, a single start can stop short of
the best fit. The fixed-buffer kernel shows the problem, because its
likelihood changes only when a whole cell enters or leaves the buffer.

```{r start-strategy}
# One kernel_prep() call per kernel
fixed_inputs <- kernel_prep(pts = pts, raster_stack = land_rast,
                            max_D = 1700, kernel = "fixed", verbose = FALSE)

# Default: one start
opt_fixed_single <- multiScale_optim(mod, fixed_inputs, verbose = FALSE)

# Screened start: scan sigma values, run short trial fits, then optimize once
set.seed(1)                    # the trial starts are jittered at random
opt_fixed <- multiScale_optim(mod, fixed_inputs, verbose = FALSE,
                              start_strategy = "screen")

# Buffer radius (m) and log-likelihood from each strategy
data.frame(start  = c("single", "screen"),
           land1  = c(opt_fixed_single$scale_est["land1", "Mean"],
                      opt_fixed$scale_est["land1", "Mean"]),
           land2  = c(opt_fixed_single$scale_est["land2", "Mean"],
                      opt_fixed$scale_est["land2", "Mean"]),
           logLik = c(logLik(opt_fixed_single$opt_mod),
                      logLik(opt_fixed$opt_mod)))
```

**How to read the output:** A higher log-likelihood is a better fit. The
single start returned the same radius for both layers and a log-likelihood
about `r round(as.numeric(logLik(opt_fixed$opt_mod) - logLik(opt_fixed_single$opt_mod)))`
units below the screened start. It had stalled. The screened start found
buffers of about `r round(opt_fixed$scale_est["land1", "Mean"])` m and
`r round(opt_fixed$scale_est["land2", "Mean"])` m.

A screened start first scans `screen_n_sigma` log-spaced sigma values for each
covariate. It then runs `screen_n_jitter` short optimizations of
`screen_maxit` iterations from randomly shifted candidates and launches one
full optimization from the best of them. Use it for the fixed-buffer kernel,
for landscape metrics, for models with several landscape covariates, and
whenever two runs disagree. For the full Gaussian model above, a screened
start returns the same estimates as the default.

You can also supply starting values through `par`. The optimizer works with
sigma divided by `max_D`, so starting `land1` at 250 m and `land2` at 500 m is
`par = c(250, 500) / kernel_inputs$unit_conv`.

# Compare models

Estimating a scale of effect uses information from the data, so each
estimated sigma counts as one parameter. The AIC that `glm()` prints for the
final model omits those parameters. `aic_tab()` and `bic_tab()` include them,
which makes models with different numbers of landscape covariates comparable.

## Compare kernels

```{r compare-kernels}
# Prepare the same data with the two remaining kernels
exp_inputs   <- kernel_prep(pts = pts, raster_stack = land_rast,
                            max_D = 1700, kernel = "exp", verbose = FALSE)
expow_inputs <- kernel_prep(pts = pts, raster_stack = land_rast,
                            max_D = 1700, kernel = "expow", verbose = FALSE)

# Refit the reduced model with each kernel
opt_exp   <- multiScale_optim(mod, exp_inputs,   verbose = FALSE)
opt_expow <- multiScale_optim(mod, expow_inputs, verbose = FALSE)

# Rank the four kernels by AICc. opt_fixed is the screened fit from above
aic_tab(list(opt, opt_exp, opt_expow, opt_fixed),
        mod_names = c("Gaussian", "Negative exponential",
                      "Exponential power", "Fixed buffer"))
```

**How to read the table:** `K` is the number of estimated parameters. The
Gaussian model has four regression coefficients and two sigma values. The
exponential power model adds a shape parameter for each covariate, which makes
eight. `LL` is the log-likelihood, `Delta_AICc` is the distance from the best
model, and `AICcWt` is the relative support for each model within this set. A
common rule treats models within 2 AICc units of the best as having comparable
support.

The Gaussian kernel ranks first, as it should for data simulated from one.
Although the exponential power kernel has the highest log-likelihood, it pays
for two extra parameters. The negative exponential kernel has little support. In practice
the kernels often lead to the same ecological conclusions, which is one reason
the Gaussian kernel is the default.

## Compare model structures

The more common question is which covariates belong in the model. Fit each
candidate, estimate its scales, and rank the set. A model without landscape
covariates needs no optimization and enters the list as an ordinary `glm`.

```{r compare-structures}
# Candidate starting models
mod_land  <- glm(counts ~ land1 + land2, family = poisson(), data = df)
mod_land1 <- glm(counts ~ land1,         family = poisson(), data = df)
mod_land2 <- glm(counts ~ land2,         family = poisson(), data = df)
mod_site  <- glm(counts ~ site,          family = poisson(), data = df)

# Estimate the scales of effect for each landscape model
opt_land  <- multiScale_optim(mod_land,  kernel_inputs, verbose = FALSE)
opt_land1 <- multiScale_optim(mod_land1, kernel_inputs, verbose = FALSE)
opt_land2 <- multiScale_optim(mod_land2, kernel_inputs, verbose = FALSE)

model_set <- list(opt_full, opt, opt_land, opt_land1, opt_land2, mod_site)
model_names <- c("site + land1 + land2 + land3", "site + land1 + land2",
                 "land1 + land2", "land1", "land2", "site")

aic_tab(model_set, mod_names = model_names)   # ranked by AICc
bic_tab(model_set, mod_names = model_names)   # ranked by BIC
```

**How to read the tables:** Both criteria separate the three models that hold
both landscape layers from the rest by more than 15 units. Neither settles the
order among those three. AICc places the data-generating model first, with the
model that drops `site` and the model that adds `land3` each about 2 units
behind. BIC penalizes parameters more heavily. It prefers the model without
`site` by a fraction of a unit and puts the `land3` model well back.

> **What this means for your study.** Information criteria tell you that the
> landscape matters here. They have less power to settle which closely related
> model is best. Weigh them together with the size and precision of each
> coefficient, the sigma intervals, and the likelihood profiles.

Compare models only when they were fitted to the same observations.
`vignette("cross-validation", package = "multiScaleR")` shows how to compare
models by how well they predict held-out data.

# Fit other model families

The workflow does not change with the model family. Prepare the inputs, fit a
starting model with the function you would normally use, and pass it to
`multiScale_optim()`.

## Model overdispersed counts

A negative binomial model adds a dispersion parameter, theta, for counts that
vary more than a Poisson model allows.

```{r negative-binomial}
# Negative binomial starting model for the running example
mod_nb <- MASS::glm.nb(counts ~ site + land1 + land2, data = df)
opt_nb <- multiScale_optim(mod_nb, kernel_inputs, verbose = FALSE)

opt_nb$scale_est          # sigma (m), nearly identical to the Poisson fit
opt_nb$opt_mod$theta      # dispersion: large values mean little overdispersion

# Is the extra parameter worth it?
aic_tab(list(opt, opt_nb), mod_names = c("Poisson", "Negative binomial"))
```

**How to read the output:** These counts were simulated from a Poisson
process, and the fit says so. Theta is large, which makes the negative
binomial distribution almost identical to the Poisson. The scales of effect do
not move, and AICc favors the Poisson model by about the cost of one
parameter. A small theta, and a negative binomial model at the top of the
table, would point to overdispersion.

## Model counts with excess zeros

A zero-inflated model has two parts. A count model describes abundance, and a
logistic model describes the probability of an excess zero, a zero that the
count model does not account for. Each part can have its own landscape
covariate and its own scale of effect. No package function simulates this
design, so the code below builds it by hand. It takes about 10 seconds, so the
vignette shows the code and loads the stored fit.

```{r zinb-fit, eval = FALSE}
set.seed(12345)
zi_rast <- sim_rast(user_seed = 999, dim = 500, resolution = 30)
zi_rast <- subset(zi_rast, c("bin1", "cont1"))   # one binary, one continuous layer

# 400 random points at least 1,000 m inside the raster edge
interior <- buffer(vect(ext(zi_rast)), -1000)
zi_pts   <- spatSample(zi_rast[[1]], size = 400, method = "random",
                       ext = ext(interior), as.points = TRUE)

# Covariates weighted at the true scales: 400 m for bin1, 200 m for cont1
truth <- kernel_prep(pts = zi_pts, raster_stack = zi_rast, max_D = 1500,
                     kernel = "gaussian", sigma = c(400, 200),
                     verbose = FALSE)$kernel_dat

# Excess zeros depend on cont1. Counts depend on bin1
excess_zero <- rbinom(400, size = 1, prob = plogis(-0.25 - 1 * truth$cont1))
abundance   <- rnbinom(400, mu = exp(0.5 + 0.75 * truth$bin1), size = 2)
zi_dat      <- data.frame(cnt = ifelse(excess_zero == 1, 0, abundance))

# Prepare the inputs without telling the package the true scales
zi_inputs <- kernel_prep(pts = zi_pts, raster_stack = zi_rast, max_D = 1500,
                         kernel = "gaussian", verbose = FALSE)
zi_df <- data.frame(zi_dat, zi_inputs$kernel_dat)

# Count model | zero-inflation model
zinb_mod <- pscl::zeroinfl(cnt ~ bin1 | cont1, dist = "negbin", data = zi_df)
zinb_opt <- multiScale_optim(zinb_mod, zi_inputs, verbose = FALSE)
```

```{r zinb-load, include = FALSE}
zinb_opt <- guide_cache$zinb_opt
```

```{r zinb-read}
round(summary(zinb_opt)$opt_scale)      # sigma (m): truth is 400 and 200
round(coef(zinb_opt$opt_mod), 2)        # truth: 0.5, 0.75, -0.25, -1
```

**How to read the output:** Both sigma intervals contain the value used to
simulate the data. The interval for `cont1`, the zero-inflation covariate, is
the wider of the two relative to its estimate. Coefficients named `count_` are
on the log scale, so `exp()` gives a multiplicative change in expected
abundance. Coefficients named `zero_` are on the logit scale and describe the
probability of an excess zero. The negative `zero_cont1` means that excess
zeros become less likely as kernel-weighted `cont1` increases. This design
uses 400 sites, four times the count example. Fit zero-inflated models with
`pscl::zeroinfl()`.

## Model binary occurrence

For presence and absence at a site, fit a binomial GLM with a logit link. The
response can take several forms.

| Response | Example | What counts as a success |
|:---------|:--------|:-------------------------|
| Numeric 0 and 1 | `present ~ ...` | 1 |
| Logical | `detected ~ ...` | `TRUE` |
| Two-level factor | `status ~ ...` | The second factor level |
| Successes and failures from repeated trials | `cbind(detections, visits - detections) ~ ...` | The first column |

The example below reduces the running counts to presence and absence.

```{r binomial}
df$present <- as.integer(df$counts > 0)    # 1 when any animal was counted
table(df$present)

mod_bin <- glm(present ~ site + land1 + land2,
               family = binomial(link = "logit"),
               data   = df)
opt_bin <- multiScale_optim(mod_bin, kernel_inputs, verbose = FALSE)

round(summary(opt_bin)$opt_scale)          # sigma, SE, and 95% limits (m)
round(exp(coef(opt_bin$opt_mod)), 2)       # odds ratios
```

**How to read the output:** The coefficients are on the logit scale, so
`exp()` gives an odds ratio. One standard deviation more kernel-weighted
`land1` multiplies the odds of occurrence by
`r round(exp(coef(opt_bin$opt_mod))["land1"], 2)`. Use `plogis()` on a linear
predictor to obtain a probability. A prediction on the response scale is the
probability of a 1. The sigma estimates resemble those from the count model,
but the standard error for `land1` is about twice as large. Presence and
absence carry less information than counts, so expect to need more sites for
the same precision.

At the estimated scales, the final model in `opt_bin$opt_mod` is an ordinary
`glm()` fit, and its coefficients match what `glm()` returns for the same
kernel-weighted covariates. The standard errors in that table treat sigma as
known. Three details help when you compare or extend a binomial model.

- `aic_tab()` treats a logical response and the same response coded 0 and 1
  as the same data.
- The default backend keeps the link and weights of your `glm()` call.
- `backend = "profile_glm"` estimates the scales and coefficients in one
  likelihood, which allows intervals that carry both sources of uncertainty
  (see `vignette("inference-contracts", package = "multiScaleR")`). For
  binomial models it accepts only the logit link, and weights must be positive
  whole numbers that count repeated observations.

## Model abundance with imperfect detection

An N-mixture model from `unmarked::pcount()` separates abundance from the
probability of detecting each individual, using repeated counts at each site.
Landscape covariates must be site covariates of the abundance model.
`sim_rast()` and `sim_dat_unmarked()` simulate rasters and repeated surveys
for this kind of design.

```{r nmix-data, fig.height = 3.5, fig.cap = "***The two simulated layers used for the `unmarked` examples.***"}
library(unmarked)

# Four simulated layers on a 10 m grid. Keep one binary and one continuous
um_rast <- subset(sim_rast(user_seed = 999, dim = 250), c("bin1", "cont2"))
plot(um_rast)

# 75 sites, 5 surveys each, individual detection probability 0.5
nmix_sim <- sim_dat_unmarked(alpha = 1,                # abundance intercept (log)
                             beta  = c(0.75, -0.75),   # effects of bin1, cont2
                             sigma = c(75, 150),       # true scales (m)
                             kernel = "gaussian", type = "count",
                             n_points = 75, n_surv = 5, det = 0.5,
                             raster_stack = um_rast, max_D = 550,
                             user_seed = 555)

nmix_inputs <- kernel_prep(pts = nmix_sim$pts, raster_stack = um_rast,
                           max_D = 550, kernel = "gaussian", verbose = FALSE)

# Counts (sites by surveys) with the kernel-weighted site covariates
nmix_umf <- unmarkedFramePCount(y = nmix_sim$y,
                                siteCovs = nmix_inputs$kernel_dat)

# Starting model: ~ detection ~ abundance
nmix_mod <- pcount(~ 1 ~ bin1 + cont2, data = nmix_umf, K = 100)
```

`pcount()` sums the likelihood over every possible abundance up to `K`.
Because the optimizer refits that model many times, this fit takes about four
minutes. The call is shown, and the stored result is loaded.

```{r nmix-optim, eval = FALSE}
opt_nmix <- multiScale_optim(fitted_mod    = nmix_mod,
                             kernel_inputs = nmix_inputs)
```

```{r nmix-load, include = FALSE}
opt_nmix <- opt_nmix_stored
# The stored fit came from this call under other object names. Show the call
# as it is written above.
opt_nmix$call <- quote(multiScale_optim(fitted_mod = nmix_mod,
                                        kernel_inputs = nmix_inputs))
```

```{r nmix-summary}
summary(opt_nmix)

# Detection is reported on the logit scale. Convert it to a probability
plogis(coef(opt_nmix$opt_mod, type = "det"))
```

**How to read the output:** The fitted model summary is the `unmarked` summary
for the final model. Abundance coefficients are on the log scale and detection
is on the logit scale. The intercept and both effects are close to the
simulated values of 1, 0.75, and -0.75, and the detection probability of
`r round(plogis(coef(opt_nmix$opt_mod, type = "det")), 2)` is close to 0.5.
Scale recovery is weaker. The interval for `cont2` contains the true
150 m, but the interval for `bin1` falls short of the true 75 m. The summary
also warns that an effective distance approaches `max_D`. Prepare the inputs
again with the larger `max_D` it suggests before you interpret these scales.

`plot()` and `plot_marginal_effects()` work as they do for a GLM. The effect
panels show expected abundance by default, and `type = "det"` shows detection
probability.

Two points matter when you compare `pcount()` models.

```{r nmix-compare}
# K in this table counts parameters: 3 abundance, 1 detection, 2 sigma
aic_tab(list(opt_nmix), mod_names = "bin1 + cont2")

# K in pcount() is the upper limit of the abundance sum. Check that the
# log-likelihood does not change when you raise it
c(K_100 = logLik(nmix_mod), K_200 = logLik(update(nmix_mod, K = 200)))
```

**How to read the output:** The two uses of the letter are unrelated. In the
table, `K` is the number of estimated parameters. Each abundance and detection
coefficient counts once, and each estimated sigma adds one. The site
abundances are summed out of the likelihood and add nothing. In `pcount()`,
`K` is a computational limit. The log-likelihood here is the same at 100 and
200, so 100 was large enough. If it changes, raise `K` and refit.

`aic_tab()` also checks that the models used the same observations. Two models
can share sites and still differ in the surveys they use when a detection
covariate has missing values, and the function stops when that happens. If a
site appears in several rows of the `unmarked` frame, as in a stacked
multi-year design, link the rows to the prepared sites with the `join_by`
argument described in `?multiScale_optim`.

## Model occupancy with imperfect detection

An occupancy model from `unmarked::occu()` uses repeated detection and
nondetection surveys. The steps are the same. This design uses 250 sites and
takes about 10 seconds, so the stored fit is loaded.

```{r occupancy, eval = FALSE}
# 250 sites, 5 surveys each. Occupancy effects on the logit scale
occ_sim <- sim_dat_unmarked(alpha = 0.25, beta = c(-0.75, 1),
                            sigma = c(225, 75),      # true scales (m)
                            kernel = "gaussian", type = "occ",
                            n_points = 250, n_surv = 5, det = 0.5,
                            raster_stack = um_rast, max_D = 800,
                            user_seed = 555)

occ_inputs <- kernel_prep(pts = occ_sim$pts, raster_stack = um_rast,
                          max_D = 800, kernel = "gaussian", verbose = FALSE)
occ_umf <- unmarkedFrameOccu(y = occ_sim$y, siteCovs = occ_inputs$kernel_dat)

# Starting model: ~ detection ~ occupancy
occ_mod <- occu(~ 1 ~ bin1 + cont2, data = occ_umf)
opt_occ <- multiScale_optim(occ_mod, occ_inputs, verbose = FALSE)
```

```{r occupancy-load, include = FALSE}
opt_occ <- guide_cache$opt_occ
```

```{r occupancy-read}
round(summary(opt_occ)$opt_scale)                 # sigma (m): truth is 225 and 75
round(coef(opt_occ$opt_mod), 2)                   # logit scale
plogis(coef(opt_occ$opt_mod, type = "det"))       # detection probability
```

**How to read the output:** Coefficients named `psi` describe occupancy on the
logit scale, and `p` is detection. The two landscape effects have the
simulated signs, with estimates to compare against the simulated -0.75 and 1.
Each sigma interval contains its true value, yet both intervals span more than
200 m. Even with 250 sites, this occupancy model locates the scale of effect
only roughly. Plan for larger samples than a count model would need, and check
the profile before you interpret an occupancy scale.

# Map the fitted model

`kernel_scale.raster()` applies each fitted kernel to the whole raster. With
`scale_center = TRUE` it standardizes the result with the mean and standard
deviation from the fitted data, so the layers match what the model saw. With
`clamp = TRUE` it holds each layer within the range observed at the survey
points.

```{r project, fig.cap = "***Layers for prediction from the reduced count model, in standard deviation units.***"}
r_scaled <- kernel_scale.raster(raster_stack = land_rast,
                                multiScaleR  = opt,     # the fitted object
                                scale_center = TRUE,    # same scaling as the model
                                clamp        = TRUE,    # stay within the fitted range
                                verbose      = FALSE)
plot(r_scaled)
```

**How to read these plots:** `land1` and `land2` are smoothed at their
estimated scales, and zero is the average survey point. The third layer,
`site`, is constant. `site` is not a raster, so the function adds a layer of
zeros to give `terra::predict()` every variable in the model. Because `site`
is centered, the map describes average `site` conditions. For other models,
set the value that defines your scenario with `site_values`. A model with
`offset(log(n_weeks))` is projected for one week unless you set, for example,
`offset_values = c(n_weeks = 4)`.

```{r predict, fig.cap = "***Expected count across the landscape, with survey points.***"}
# Expected count in every raster cell
pred <- terra::predict(r_scaled, opt$opt_mod, type = "response")
plot(pred, main = "Expected count")
points(pts, pch = 19, cex = 0.5, col = "red")
```

**How to read this map:** Each cell holds the count the model expects for a
survey point at that location. Values near the border rest on kernels that
extend past the raster edge, so read them with caution.

For an `unmarked` model, call the `unmarked` prediction method through the
`fun` argument and name the part of the model you want.

```{r predict-unmarked, fig.height = 5.5, fig.cap = "***Expected abundance from the N-mixture model, with its standard error and 95% confidence limits.***"}
um_scaled <- kernel_scale.raster(raster_stack = um_rast, multiScaleR = opt_nmix,
                                 scale_center = TRUE, clamp = TRUE,
                                 verbose = FALSE)

# type = "state" is abundance for pcount() and occupancy probability for occu()
predict_state <- function(model, data, ...) {
  unmarked::predict(model, type = "state", newdata = data, ...)
}
abundance_map <- terra::predict(um_scaled, opt_nmix$opt_mod,
                                fun = predict_state, na.rm = TRUE)
plot(abundance_map)
```

**How to read these maps:** `Predicted` is expected abundance per site, `SE`
is its standard error, and `lower` and `upper` are 95% confidence limits. The
map shows animals present, not animals you would expect to count, and the
limits treat the estimated scales as known.

By default the kernel is applied over a window sized from the kernel itself,
which can differ slightly from the `max_D` buffer used in fitting. Set
`match_buffer = TRUE` to use the fitting buffer. That option needs rasters
with a projected coordinate reference system at the resolution you prepared,
and `na.rm = TRUE`. It works with either smoothing method, `fft = TRUE` or
`fft = FALSE`. `vignette("spatial_projection_clamping", package = "multiScaleR")`
covers clamping and prediction beyond the sampled conditions.

# Quick reference

```{r quick-reference, eval = FALSE}
library(multiScaleR)
library(terra)

# 1. Understand the kernel
plot_kernel(sigma = 300, kernel = "gaussian", add_label = FALSE)
kernel_dist(sigma = 300, kernel = "gaussian")      # radius with 90% of the weight

# 2. Prepare the data
data("landscape_counts"); data("surv_pts")
dat       <- landscape_counts
pts       <- vect(surv_pts)
land_rast <- rast(system.file("extdata", "landscape.tif",
                              package = "multiScaleR"))
kernel_inputs <- kernel_prep(pts = pts, raster_stack = land_rast,
                             max_D = 1700, kernel = "gaussian")

# 3. Fit a starting model and estimate the scales
df  <- data.frame(dat, kernel_inputs$kernel_dat)
mod <- glm(counts ~ site + land1 + land2, family = poisson(), data = df)
opt <- multiScale_optim(fitted_mod = mod, kernel_inputs = kernel_inputs)

# 4. Read and check the fit
summary(opt)                                # sigma, distance, coefficients, warnings
summary(opt, profile = TRUE)                # profile-likelihood limits for sigma
kernel_dist(opt)                            # effective distance (map units)
plot(opt)                                   # fitted kernels
plot(opt, prob = 0.99, add_label = FALSE)   # 99% radius, no text under panels
plot_marginal_effects(opt)                  # expected response across covariates
plot(profile_sigma(opt, n_pts = 15))        # is each scale identified?

# 5. Guard against a stalled search
fixed_inputs <- kernel_prep(pts = pts, raster_stack = land_rast,
                            max_D = 1700, kernel = "fixed")
set.seed(1)
opt_fixed <- multiScale_optim(mod, fixed_inputs, start_strategy = "screen")

# 6. Compare models (each sigma counts as a parameter)
mod_land <- glm(counts ~ land1 + land2, family = poisson(), data = df)
opt_land <- multiScale_optim(mod_land, kernel_inputs)
aic_tab(list(opt, opt_land), mod_names = c("site + land1 + land2",
                                           "land1 + land2"))

# 7. Other families: same workflow, different starting model
mod_nb     <- MASS::glm.nb(counts ~ site + land1 + land2, data = df)
df$present <- as.integer(df$counts > 0)
mod_bin    <- glm(present ~ site + land1 + land2,
                  family = binomial(link = "logit"), data = df)
opt_nb     <- multiScale_optim(mod_nb,  kernel_inputs)
opt_bin    <- multiScale_optim(mod_bin, kernel_inputs)
# pscl::zeroinfl(cnt ~ bin1 | cont1, dist = "negbin", data = zi_df)
# unmarked::pcount(~ 1 ~ bin1 + cont2, data = nmix_umf, K = 100)
# unmarked::occu(~ 1 ~ bin1 + cont2, data = occ_umf)

# 8. Map the fitted model
r_scaled <- kernel_scale.raster(raster_stack = land_rast, multiScaleR = opt,
                                scale_center = TRUE, clamp = TRUE)
pred <- terra::predict(r_scaled, opt$opt_mod, type = "response")
```

## Summary of key functions

| Function | Purpose |
|:---------|:--------|
| `plot_kernel()` | Draw a kernel for a chosen sigma, without a fitted model |
| `kernel_dist()` | Convert sigma to the distance that holds a chosen share of the kernel weight |
| `kernel_prep()` | Extract raster values around each survey point and prepare the optimizer inputs |
| `estimate_multiscale_ram()` | Estimate memory use and a safe number of parallel workers |
| `multiScale_optim()` | Estimate sigma for each landscape covariate together with the model coefficients |
| `summary()` | Report sigma, effective distance, the model table, and warnings |
| `plot()` | Draw the fitted kernels |
| `plot_marginal_effects()` | Draw the expected response across each covariate |
| `profile_sigma()` | Show model support across sigma for each covariate |
| `aic_tab()`, `bic_tab()` | Rank models, counting each estimated sigma as a parameter |
| `kernel_scale.raster()` | Apply the fitted kernels to a raster for mapping and prediction |
| `sim_rast()`, `sim_dat()`, `sim_dat_unmarked()` | Simulate rasters and responses with known scales of effect |
